\title{Predicting hydropower unit commitment in Tokke--Vinje:\\
from feature engineering to a first-principles optimiser\\[4pt]
\large TDT4173 Modern Machine Learning in Practice --- SINTEF task --- Group \groupno}
\author{Anders Bærheim (student ID 114407)\\ Peter Klivnoy (student ID 114439)\\[6pt]
Kaggle team: \kaggleteam}
\date{November 2026}

\graphicspath{{./}{../report/}}

\begin{document}
\maketitle

\begin{abstract}
We predict, for every hour of a one-week scheduling case and each of the 14 generating units of the
Tokke--Vinje hydropower system, the probability that SINTEF's SHOP optimiser commits the unit. The
work followed three tracks. \emph{Track A} engineered features for gradient-boosted trees ---
economic spreads between price and water value, terminal water values, a count model over hours-on
per unit-week, hourly block structure, a long (case, hour, unit) format --- reaching 0.9638 micro
ROC-AUC in walk-forward validation and 0.98058 on the public leaderboard. \emph{Track B} starts from
the observation that the labels are the output of a known optimisation problem whose inputs we hold
in full: we rebuilt SHOP's weekly problem as a linear programme from the SHOP-ready topology file and
use its solution \emph{only as features} for LightGBM, which scores 0.9912 in walk-forward
validation, improving every fold and all 14 units over Track A, and \kagglelp{} on the public
leaderboard. \emph{Track C} trains a sequence neural network --- temporal convolution, a
bidirectional GRU along each unit's week and attention across units --- on 83 base features and 16
closed-form physics features derived from the generator efficiency curves, with no solver; it scores
\textbf{\kagglenn{}} on the public leaderboard. Tracks B and C are our two selected predictions. Four
predictor types compared on identical features show that Track B's gain comes from the optimiser
features rather than from the learner.
\end{abstract}

\section{The task and the data}
\label{sec:r-task}

Short-term hydropower scheduling decides, hour by hour, which generating units run and at what
level. SINTEF's SHOP software solves this as a mixed-integer optimisation problem; the InterOpt
project asks whether a machine-learning model can predict SHOP's on/off (unit-commitment)
decisions from the inputs, to speed up or warm-start the optimiser.

The Tokke--Vinje watercourse has 17 reservoirs, 9 plants and 14 units (1{,}000\,MW installed). Each
\emph{case} is a 168-hour week starting at 00:00 UTC; cases start every day, so consecutive cases
overlap by 144 hours. There are 2{,}922 labelled cases (2015-01-01 to 2022-12-31) and 725 test cases
(2023-01-01 to 2024-12-25). The model must output, for each test case, unit and hour, a value in
$[0,1]$: the probability that the unit is on. The metric is micro-averaged ROC-AUC over every
(case, hour, unit) cell --- 6.9M labelled cells and 1.7M test cells --- so probabilities must be
comparable across units as well as ordered within each unit-week.

\paragraph{Three tracks.} The work ran in three tracks, and the report follows them through every
section. \emph{Track A} (Peter Klivnoy) engineered features for gradient-boosted trees
and produced our first submission (0.98058). \emph{Track B} (Peter Klivnoy) rebuilt the
optimisation problem that generated the labels as a linear programme and uses its solution as
features for LightGBM. \emph{Track C} (Anders Bærheim) built closed-form physics features from the
generator curves and a sequence neural network over each case. Tracks B and C are the two selected
predictions (Short notebooks 1 and 2).

\section{Exploratory data analysis}
\label{sec:r-eda}

Five rounds of EDA shaped every later decision. This section is organised by the six activities in the course's EDA list; we did all six.

% ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection{Search domain knowledge}
\label{sec:eda-domain}

We read the task statement, the dataset documentation and the SHOP-format topology file (whose
attributes are defined in the SHOP documentation), and used the standard economics of hydropower
scheduling. The facts that mattered:

\begin{itemize}
\item \textbf{Water value is an opportunity cost.} Water released now cannot be sold later. A unit is
  worth running when the price exceeds the value of the water it uses, the reservoir's
  \emph{water value} (EUR/MWh). The dispatch condition is therefore the \emph{spread} between price
  and water value, not the price alone.
\item \textbf{The week has a boundary condition.} A weekly schedule values the water left at the end
  of the week at the \emph{terminal} water value; the documentation states which day's value that is.
\item \textbf{Starting a unit costs money} (start/stop costs in the topology file), so units run in
  contiguous blocks rather than hour by hour.
\item \textbf{The system is a cascade.} Water released upstream flows into downstream reservoirs and
  plants (Figure~\ref{fig:r-topo}); a plant's decision depends on the reservoirs above and below it.
\item \textbf{Identical units share a penstock} at Tokke (four units) and Vinje (three), so which one
  starts first is a matter of hydraulic losses and tie-breaking, not of different machines.
\item \textbf{Norwegian inflow is dominated by snowmelt} in May--June; reservoirs are drawn down
  through winter and refilled in summer.
\end{itemize}

\subsection{Understand how the data was generated}
\label{sec:eda-generated}

\begin{itemize}
\item \textbf{The labels are optimiser output.} Every case was solved by SHOP v17.17 on the
  Tokke--Vinje model described by the topology file. The labels are therefore a deterministic
  function of the inputs we hold, not noisy observations of the real plant.
\item \textbf{Cases are rolling.} A new case starts every day, so consecutive cases share 144
  wall-clock hours, solved from almost the same state. The same hour solved one day later gets a
  \emph{different} decision 12\% of the time (18\% for Tokke and Vinje; Figure~\ref{fig:r-selfagree}):
  the decision depends on the whole horizon, including the end-of-week boundary, not only on the
  hour. This label self-disagreement explains 78\% of the variance in per-unit difficulty of our first
  baseline. It also means random row splits leak (Section~\ref{sec:r-val}).
\item \textbf{The water values are synthetic} (file name and documentation), one per reservoir per
  day. For a case starting on day $d$ the documentation defines the initial value at $d$ and the
  final (terminal) value at $d+7$ 00:00. We first read the terminal value one day late and found the
  off-by-one by rereading the documentation.
\item \textbf{Two storage series are invented:} Hyljelihyl and Vatjern have no historical records and
  are set to 50\% full throughout.
\item \textbf{The storage series is observed, not planned:} it is the reservoir level at the start of
  each day, so the level at the end of a case reflects decisions taken during it
  (``post-decision'' information, Section~\ref{sec:eda-clean}).
\item \textbf{SHOP's conventions can be recovered from the labels.} Rebuilding the generator
  (Track B, Section~\ref{sec:fe-lp}) required three conventions the documentation does not state ---
  how water values are converted to a value per cubic metre, how river costs are read, how identical
  units are ordered --- and we measured each of them from the labels (Figure~\ref{fig:r-thr}).
\end{itemize}

\begin{figure}[H]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=0.6\linewidth]{figures/eda2_01_label_self_agreement.png}
\caption{Agreement between consecutive cases on identical wall-clock hours, per unit.}
\label{fig:r-selfagree}
\end{figure}

\subsection{Check if the data is intuitive}
\label{sec:eda-intuitive}

Most series behave as domain knowledge predicts. Inflow peaks in May--June at about 8 times the
winter level, and storage follows the expected annual fill and drawdown
(Figure~\ref{fig:r-inflow-storage}). The system water value tracks price but is much smoother,
as an expected \emph{future} value should be. Commitment has a double-hump daily pattern (trough 0.46
at night, peaks 0.55 at the morning and evening ramps) and almost no weekday pattern
(Figure~\ref{fig:r-hod}).

One fact is counter-intuitive: \textbf{2022 has the highest prices ($\sim$211\,EUR/MWh) and the lowest
on-rate (0.34)} (Figure~\ref{fig:r-year-wv}, left), and raw price correlates \emph{negatively} with
commitment ($-0.19$). The resolution is in the right panel: water values rose with prices, so high
prices did not mean a high \emph{spread}; 2022 was a scarce-water year in which SHOP conserved water.
Measured within each week, price correlates positively ($+0.26$ for the within-week z-score). The
data is consistent once read through the opportunity cost of water.

\caption{Left: mean total inflow by month (snowmelt in May--June). Right: daily storage of the three

\end{figure}

\subsection{Explore individual features}
\label{sec:eda-individual}

\paragraph{Target.} On-rates range from 26\% (Vinje G3) to 75\% (Lio G1): fourteen differently
balanced problems pooled by one metric (Figure~\ref{fig:r-target}, left). Most unit-weeks are flat:
Haukeli never switches in 81\% of weeks, Vesle Kjela in 75\%, Byrte in 74\% (right); within a week
commitments come in 1.2--2.7 contiguous blocks, $P(\text{on}_t \mid \text{on}_{t-1}) = 0.995$. The
units are not stationary: Haukeli's on-rate falls from 0.87 (2015) to 0.14 (2022) and Songa swings
$0.30 \to 0.71 \to 0.12$ (Figure~\ref{fig:r-instab}).

\begin{figure}[H]
\centering
\begin{subfigure}{0.49\linewidth}\includegraphics[width=\linewidth]{figures/eda_01_unit_on_rate.png}\end{subfigure}
\begin{subfigure}{0.49\linewidth}\includegraphics[width=\linewidth]{figures/eda2_04_flat_vs_mixed.png}\end{subfigure}
\caption{Left: on-rate per unit, 2015--2022. Right: share of unit-weeks that never switch.}
\label{fig:r-target}
\end{figure}

\begin{figure}[H]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=0.62\linewidth]{figures/eda2_06_yearly_instability.png}
\caption{On-rate per unit by year, sorted by instability.}
\label{fig:r-instab}
\end{figure}

\paragraph{Price.} Stable at 9--43\,EUR/MWh until 2020, then the 2021--22 energy crisis; the test
period 2023--24 sits between the two regimes and contains negative prices in 2.2\% of hours
(Figure~\ref{fig:r-price}).

\begin{figure}[H]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=0.85\linewidth]{figures/eda_05_price_timeseries.png}
\caption{Daily mean day-ahead price, test window shaded.}
\label{fig:r-price}
\end{figure}

\paragraph{Inflow, storage, water value.} Strongly seasonal (Figure~\ref{fig:r-inflow-storage}).
Raw levels are weak predictors because they confound the season: every reservoir is full in June.
Normalised against the same time of year, they become the strongest univariate correlates in the
project --- storage's seasonal percentile $+0.54$, inflow's trailing-year mean $+0.33$
(Figure~\ref{fig:r-slow}, Section~\ref{sec:eda-pairs}).

\paragraph{Constraints.} Minimum-volume constraints bind for exactly three reservoirs and only from
July to October. Minimum flow is positive in every hour for five of the six constrained rivers, so a
binary ``constrained'' flag would be constant; the information is in the level and its changes.

% ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection{Explore pairs and groups of features}
\label{sec:eda-pairs}

\paragraph{Units together.} Units at one plant correlate 0.8--0.96, and Tokke and Vinje correlate
0.8--0.9 with each other because Vinje's discharge feeds the reservoir Tokke draws from
(Figure~\ref{fig:r-units}, left). Identical units follow a near-strict merit order (right): one Tokke
unit on is G1 99\% of the time, two are G1+G3 94\%; knowing how many units are on predicts exactly
which ones with 97.8\% (Tokke) and 99.9\% (Vinje) accuracy.

\begin{figure}[H]
\centering
\begin{subfigure}{0.36\linewidth}\includegraphics[width=\linewidth]{figures/eda_02_unit_correlation_heatmap.png}\end{subfigure}
\begin{subfigure}{0.63\linewidth}\includegraphics[width=\linewidth]{figures/eda2_03_merit_order.png}\end{subfigure}
\caption{Left: correlation of the units' daily on-fraction, blocks by plant. Right:
$P(\text{unit on} \mid k \text{ units on at the plant})$ for Tokke and Vinje.}
\label{fig:r-units}
\end{figure}

\paragraph{Price with water value.} The spread price $-$ water value of the feeding reservoir
correlates with commitment more strongly than either component, for every unit
(Figure~\ref{fig:r-spread}, left). Price helps only relative to its week: subtracting the case mean
flips its correlation from $-0.185$ to $+0.183$ and dividing by the case's standard deviation gives
$+0.263$ (right). The spread must \emph{not} be normalised the same way ($+0.241$ raw, $+0.114$
z-scored): it is already relative.

\begin{figure}[H]
\centering
\begin{subfigure}{0.49\linewidth}\includegraphics[width=\linewidth]{figures/eda2_05_spread_vs_components.png}\end{subfigure}
\begin{subfigure}{0.49\linewidth}\includegraphics[width=\linewidth]{figures/eda3_01_normalisation_components.png}\end{subfigure}
\caption{Left: $|$correlation$|$ with commitment of price, own water value and their spread, per
unit. Right: correlation of five price transformations with commitment.}
\label{fig:r-spread}
\end{figure}

\paragraph{Groups of series.} The 17 water-value columns share one factor (PC1 explains 91\% of
their variance); inflow needs 3 components for 90\%, storage 7 (Figure~\ref{fig:r-pca}). The useful
decomposition is a system-wide level plus each reservoir's deviation from it; the deviation is the
strongest of the three for five units but useless for Tokke, whose reservoir tracks the system.

\begin{figure}[H]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=0.9\linewidth]{figures/eda3_03_pca_dimensionality.png}
\caption{Variance explained by principal components within each family of series.}
\label{fig:r-pca}
\end{figure}

\paragraph{Across time.} The terminal water value correlates $-0.41$ with case-level commitment
against $-0.26$ for the initial value, and the two differ in 93\% of case/reservoir pairs
(Figure~\ref{fig:r-time}, left). Price correlates with commitment most weakly at the current hour
and more strongly at leads and lags of several days (right): SHOP plans the whole week. Normalising
the slow series against the same time of year raises their correlation 1.3--2.6$\times$
(Figure~\ref{fig:r-slow}).

\begin{figure}[H]
\centering
\begin{subfigure}{0.49\linewidth}\includegraphics[width=\linewidth]{figures/eda3_05_terminal_water_value.png}\end{subfigure}
\begin{subfigure}{0.49\linewidth}\includegraphics[width=\linewidth]{figures/eda3b_01_leadlag_corrected.png}\end{subfigure}
\caption{Left: initial and terminal water value against case-level commitment. Right: correlation
of commitment with price $k$ hours earlier or later, within the case horizon.}
\label{fig:r-time}
\end{figure}

\begin{figure}[H]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\linewidth]{figures/eda3b_03_slow_series_transforms.png}
\caption{Seventeen backward-looking transformations each of storage, water value and inflow, ranked
by correlation with commitment.}

\subsection{Clean up features}
\label{sec:eda-clean}

\begin{table}[H]
\centering\small
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{lY}
\toprule
check & action \\
\midrule
missing values & none in any core or extended file; reservoir names consistent across files \\
constant series & storage of Hyljelihyl and Vatjern is fixed at 50\% (no records): dropped \\
leakage & \texttt{total\_calculation\_time} (SHOP's solve time) exists only for labelled cases and
  describes the solution: excluded from all features \\
availability & every feature file covers all 725 test cases (price to 2025-12, inflow to 2025-10,
  storage and water value to 2025-01-01); labels end in 2022, so no feature may use past labels.
  The terminal water value of the last test case (2024-12-25) is the file's final row \\
redundant scaling & normalising a single column (e.g.\ storage by reservoir size) is a no-op for
  tree models; scaling was only applied where columns are combined \\
uninformative encodings & a binary ``min-flow active'' flag is constant for five of six rivers: the
  level is used instead \\
post-decision information & end-of-week storage reflects the decisions being predicted. It is legal
  (the files cover the test period) and was used in Track A; Track B shows it is not needed
  (Section~\ref{sec:fe-select}) \\
unit identity & plant names are sanitised for column names (\texttt{Vesle Kjela}) and mapped back
  from the topology for the submission header \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}
\caption{Data cleaning.}
\label{tab:r-clean}
\end{table}

\subsection{Training versus test period}
\label{sec:eda-shift}

We measured which past period resembles the test set instead of assuming it: a classifier separates
each half-year's cases from the 2023--24 test cases using case-level inputs (price level,
volatility, negative-price share, water value, spread, fill, inflow). 2021-H2 is the hardest to
separate (AUC 0.785), then 2022-H2 (0.879); every other half-year is above 0.95
(Figure~\ref{fig:r-adv}). We report these two \emph{test-like folds} separately in validation.

\begin{figure}[H]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=0.72\linewidth]{figures/physics_06_adversarial.png}
\caption{Adversarial validation: how easily each half-year's cases are told apart from the test
cases. Lower is more test-like; 0.5 would be indistinguishable.}
\label{fig:r-adv}
\end{figure}

\midrule

terminal water value is the week's boundary condition & terminal features; the LP's end-of-week value \\

\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}
\end{table}

\section{Validation methodology}
\label{sec:r-val}

\paragraph{Random splits leak.} A random row split scores 0.957 with the same model that scores 0.835
on a held-out year: rows from one week are near-duplicates, and consecutive weeks share 144 hours at
88\% label agreement. Random \emph{case} splits still inflate by $+0.105$. Every number in
this report therefore comes from a temporal split.

\paragraph{Walk-forward.} The reference protocol has six half-year folds from 2020-H1
to 2022-H2; each trains on every case starting before the fold and scores the six months after.
Earlier stages used a single held-out year (2021, the most test-like year) or four-fold
rolling-origin CV; we judged changes on the per-fold sign pattern, since fold-to-fold variation (SD
up to 0.06) dwarfs most feature effects. A rotating-block scheme was built and rejected: training on
both sides of the held-out block measures interpolation, while the test set requires extrapolation.
Experiments train on every third case (``stride 3''); submissions train on all cases.

% =============================================================================================
\section{Feature engineering}
\label{sec:r-fe}

We used two types of feature engineering: \emph{feature extraction} (new features
built from the raw series, Sections~\ref{sec:fe-econ}, \ref{sec:fe-lp} and~\ref{sec:fe-phys}) and
\emph{feature selection} (Section~\ref{sec:fe-select}).

% ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection{Feature extraction I: economic and structural features (Track A)}
\label{sec:fe-econ}

Twenty feature themes were built and screened, following the EDA's rules:
case-relative price, raw spreads, seasonally normalised slow series, a system factor plus
reservoir deviations, multi-hop topology for unit-to-reservoir mapping.

\begin{table}[H]
\centering\small
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{lYL{2.3cm}}
\toprule
family & what it computes & effect \\
\midrule
spread & price $-$ water value of the reservoir feeding each plant, positive part, system spread & $+0.075$ \\
terminal water value & value at the end of the week; price $-$ terminal value; per-plant terminal spreads; slope & $+0.034$; day fixed: $+0.006$ \\

% ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection{Feature extraction II: a first-principles optimiser as a feature generator (Track B)}
\label{sec:fe-lp}

Track A approximated SHOP with hand-made features. But the labels are the output of one
deterministic optimiser, and every input it used is in our data --- the topology file is SHOP-ready.
So we rebuilt the optimisation problem itself (\texttt{src/shoplite.py}; Short notebook 1) and use
its solution as features. The LP is a \textbf{feature extractor only}: its output is never
submitted; every prediction comes from the learned model.

\paragraph{The linear programme.} One per case, the LP relaxation of SHOP's weekly unit-commitment
problem, solved with HiGHS (dual simplex; building and solving take 8\,s per case on one core on
average, 2--25\,s for individual cases; SHOP's own recorded solve times are a median 52\,s, mean
147\,s):
\[
\max\ \sum_t \lambda_t \big(P_t - L_t\big) \;-\; \text{start/stop costs} \;-\; \text{river, bypass, spill costs}
\;-\; \text{penalties} \;+\; \sum_r \omega_r V_{r,T}
\]
subject to hourly water balance in all 17 reservoirs, the Vest-Vassdraget river junction and the
Songa tunnel junction; reservoir bounds; minimum volume and minimum flow (soft, heavily penalised);
for every unit an on/off variable $u\in[0,1]$ carrying the minimum block ($q_{\min}$, $p_{\min}$)
plus segments of the concave envelope of its PQ curve at the case's initial head (turbine efficiency
interpolated between the reference-head curves, times generator efficiency); start/stop variables
with the topology's costs; and main-tunnel and shared-penstock friction $L_t$ as a convex
piecewise-linear cubic in plant flow. $\lambda_t$ is the price and $\omega_r$ the terminal value of
water. The LP's duals give the hourly shadow price of water in each reservoir, from which each unit's
\emph{local water value} (EUR/MWh) and its margin, price $-$ local water value, follow.
Simplifications against SHOP: heads frozen at their initial levels, lossless tunnels between
reservoirs, and an unknown initial on/off state.

\paragraph{Three conventions measured from the labels.} \textbf{Terminal water value:} in weeks where
a unit switches, its on-hour and off-hour prices bracket the threshold SHOP used; regressing that
threshold on terminal water values gives $\approx 1.0\times$ the feeding reservoir's value and
$\approx 0\times$ the downstream value (Figure~\ref{fig:r-thr}; Byrte slope 0.98, $R^2$ 0.99), so one
Mm\textsuperscript{3} in reservoir $r$ is valued as
$\omega_r=\sum_k \mathrm{WV}(\text{reservoir feeding }k)\cdot \mathrm{conv}_k$ over the plants $k$ on
its way to the sea. \textbf{River flow cost:} \texttt{flow\_cost\_curve} read as total cost per hour
(marginal cost = slope) rather than as a marginal cost lifted Kjela's raw AUC from 0.70 to 0.96.
\textbf{Sibling order:} the merit order from the EDA is imposed as
$u_{\text{G1}}\ge u_{\text{G3}}\ge u_{\text{G4}}\ge u_{\text{G2}}$ at Tokke and
$u_{\text{G1}}\ge u_{\text{G2}}\ge u_{\text{G3}}$ at Vinje.

\begin{figure}[H]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\linewidth]{figures/physics_01_threshold_vs_water_value.png}
\caption{Implied price threshold in every mixed week against the terminal water value of the
reservoir feeding the plant. Points lie on $y=x$: each plant breaks even at its own reservoir's
water value.}
\label{fig:r-thr}
\end{figure}

\paragraph{LP versus MILP as a feature.} Solving with binary $u$ gave a raw AUC of 0.941 against the
relaxation's 0.967 on the same 59-case sample: a 0/1 schedule loses the graded information about how
close each hour is to the margin. The relaxation is the better feature.

\paragraph{The 61 features.} One row per (case, hour, unit):
\texttt{lp\_} --- the LP solution (commitment $u$, power, flow), its temporal context (rolling
windows, run lengths, weekly and daily means, number of units on at the plant), the local water
value and margin, and the reservoir trajectories; \texttt{ec\_} --- price level, rank and z-score
within the week, spread to the terminal water value, season, inflow; \texttt{cn\_} --- the
constraint series; \texttt{st\_} --- the observed storage trajectory; \texttt{s\_} --- unit identity
and static attributes.

% ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection{Feature extraction III: closed-form physics features for a neural network (Track C)}
\label{sec:fe-phys}

Track C builds 99 features per (case, unit, hour) for a sequence model (Short notebook 2). The 83
base features follow the same EDA findings as Track A:

\begin{table}[H]
\centering\small
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{lrY}
\toprule
group & $n$ & content \\
\midrule
economic core & 9 & margin = price $-$ terminal water value of the intake reservoirs; at the initial value; share of positive hours; daily and rolling (12\,h, 24\,h min/max) views \\
price & 18 & level, within-week z-score and rank, within-day rank and position, daily spread, rolling means, lags and leads of 1/3/6\,h, price minus the mean of the remaining hours \\
water value & 9 & intake and downstream values, change over the week, daily path and its volatility, a margin against the whole cascade's water value \\
state & 9 & fill of the intake, storage and downstream reservoirs, system fill, five large reservoirs \\
inflow & 5 & weekly inflow to the plant's storage, relative to its size, system inflow, its anomaly against the 1958--2014 climatology, hourly system inflow \\
constraints & 9 & minimum flow on six rivers; distance of three reservoirs to their minimum volume \\
volume path & 8 & observed storage changes over the week and implied releases (post-decision information) \\
unit & 8 & identity, $p_{\min}$, $p_{\max}$, start cost, position in the plant, number of siblings, head, hour index \\
calendar & 5 & local hour and weekday, season, Norwegian holidays \\
plant context & 3 & system-mean margin, the unit's margin relative to it, rank across units \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}
\caption{Track C base features.}
\end{table}

\paragraph{Physics features without a solver.} Sixteen features are derived in closed form from each
generator's efficiency curves at the plant head (minus friction losses, times generator efficiency,
reduced to a concave envelope):
\begin{itemize}
\item \textbf{break-even prices} at minimum, full and marginal load --- the intake water value scaled
  by how much less efficient that operating point is than the plant's best one --- and the margins of
  price over them;
\item a \textbf{weekly water budget}: hours of full-plant flow the reservoirs feeding the plant can
  afford (storage above the minimum volume plus inflow), and hours it is \emph{forced} to run because
  the intake would otherwise overflow;
\item a \textbf{greedy schedule}: the plant runs in its $k$ best-margin hours, $k$ the number of
  positive-margin hours clipped between the forced and affordable hours; whether each hour is in it
  and how far from the cut-off;
\item \textbf{block economics}: for each run of positive-margin hours, its length and profit at full
  load against the start cost, and for each negative run, whether idling at $p_{\min}$ is cheaper than
  stopping and restarting.
\end{itemize}
These approximate, hour by hour, what Track B's LP computes jointly. They add $+0.004$ to the yearly
cross-validated AUC of the network in its original run (0.9697 $\to$ 0.9740; Section~\ref{sec:pred-nn}),
most of it on 2021 (0.9514 $\to$ 0.9658), the most test-like year (Section~\ref{sec:eda-shift}).

folds (stride 3; \texttt{src/predictor\_comparison.py}):

\item \textbf{random forest} --- 200 bagged trees, \texttt{min\_samples\_leaf} 100, $\sqrt{p}$

is rolling-origin; walk-forward is six half-year folds; yearly CV is Track C's expanding window
(2019--2022).}
\label{tab:r-all}
\end{table}

\paragraph{Terms in the table.} A \emph{pointwise} model predicts each unit-hour directly; a
\emph{count model} predicts how many hours a unit runs in the week. \emph{Allocation} gives a unit its
predicted hours in the hours with the highest spread. A \emph{stacked two-stage} model fits per-unit
residual models on top of the joint model; \emph{gated} applies them only to units where they helped
on the previous year. \emph{Count-budget augmentation} adds the difference between the predicted count
and each hour's spread rank to the pointwise model's logits. \emph{Multi-horizon} count features are
trailing and forward windows. The \emph{compact distilled} architecture passes five count-model
outputs per unit to the pointwise model instead of hundreds of raw features, and the \emph{binned head}
is a single 6-class model over bins of hours on. The \emph{unit-resolved} variant replaces per-plant
columns with the unit's own, upstream and downstream views; the \emph{stationarised} one replaces
drifting level features with ratios. \emph{Water-balance fixes} correct the storage accounting of the
four worst units (Songa, Haukeli, Lio, Hogga). \emph{Unit masking} blanks a block of features for units
outside a chosen set. \emph{Block allocation} forces each unit's hours into one contiguous window.

Three architectural ideas carried Track A. Joint modelling of the correlated units (0.647 $\to$
0.687). A count model over hours-on per unit-week: given the true count, allocating hours by spread
reaches 0.977, so the hard part is one number per unit-week; the count model first augmented and
later only ranked features, because forwarding its predictions cost 0.008. And the long
format, which made unit-specific features affordable.

\subsection{Track C: a sequence neural network}
\label{sec:pred-nn}

Each case is one sample: an input of 14 units $\times$ 168 hours $\times$ 99 features and a target of
14 $\times$ 168 commitments. The network, UCNet (244{,}161 parameters), mirrors the structure the EDA
found:
\begin{itemize}
\item a two-layer input projection to width 96, concatenated with a learned 16-dimensional embedding
  of the unit;
\item a residual temporal convolution (two layers, kernel 5, the second dilated) and a residual
  two-layer bidirectional GRU along the 168 hours of each unit --- commitments come in blocks;
\item residual multi-head self-attention (4 heads) across the 14 units at each hour --- units share
  water and are coupled through the cascade;
\item a two-layer head giving one logit per unit-hour.
\end{itemize}
Inputs are scaled per feature (median, 10--90\% range, clipped at $\pm 8$). Training minimises binary
cross-entropy over all unit-hours with AdamW and a one-cycle learning-rate schedule, 20 epochs, batches
of 32 cases; the submission averages three seeds' probabilities.

\paragraph{Validation.} Track C used an expanding window by year: train on cases starting more than 7
days before 1 January of year $Y$ (consecutive cases overlap, so the gap prevents leakage), score
year $Y$. The figures in this subsection are from the network's original run, with one seed; the
selected prediction comes from a later run of the same model in Short notebook 2
(Section~\ref{sec:r-sub}).

Track B is ahead in every year. Its lead is largest in 2021 ($+0.028$), the year that most resembles

which is why Short notebook 1 holds our best score.

\paragraph{Constants of the LP.} The optimiser in Short notebook 1 also contains fixed numbers that are
model constants rather than learning hyperparameters: unit conversions ($K = 0.0036$\,Mm\textsuperscript{3}
per m\textsuperscript{3}/s for one hour; $P = 9.81\cdot10^{-3}\,H Q \eta$\,MW); deficit penalties of
5{,}000\,EUR per m\textsuperscript{3}/s$\cdot$h of missing minimum flow and $10^5$\,EUR per
Mm\textsuperscript{3} of missing minimum volume, set by hand so that the constraints are expensive to
break but every case stays feasible (not tuned); and the three conventions measured from the labels
(Section~\ref{sec:fe-lp}). All physical data (curves, costs, limits) is read from the topology file.

% =============================================================================================
\section{Model interpretation}
\label{sec:r-interp}

\subsection{Track A: what the trees learned}

The pruned 15 features are all economic quantities --- spreads, margins, break-even hours, the
share of capacity a spread justifies --- with topology used only to pick \emph{which} water value
and \emph{which} capacity; no raw price, storage, inflow or calendar column survived. The
single most important feature of the early model, by a factor of 14, was the binary
``price $>$ system water value'': SHOP's dispatch condition, rediscovered
(Figure~\ref{fig:r-imp-a}). In the count model the top feature was the system storage change over
the week --- released water, i.e.\ production --- and the binding-constraint term
$\min(\text{hours of water}, \text{hours profitable})$. Hourly-varying features
held 96\% of the gain: micro-AUC rewards ranking hours \emph{within} a week, which a case-level
constant cannot do.

\begin{figure}[H]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=0.62\linewidth]{figures/iter1_02_feature_importance.png}
\caption{Track A, first feature iteration: gain importance. The binary spread sign --- SHOP's own
dispatch condition --- dominates.}
\label{fig:r-imp-a}
\end{figure}

\subsection{Track B: the model leans on the optimiser}

\paragraph{Ablation.} Removing one feature group at a time on the same folds
(Figure~\ref{fig:r-abl}): without the LP features the same learner scores 0.9483 --- \emph{below}
Track A --- so the gain is neither LightGBM nor the feature engineering. The LP features plus unit
identity alone reach 0.9897. Removing the observed storage trajectory changes nothing (0.9910 vs
0.9912): the model uses only information available before the week starts, unlike Track A's best
features.

\begin{figure}[H]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=0.72\linewidth]{figures/physics_04_ablation.png}
\caption{Ablation: mean walk-forward micro-AUC with one feature group removed.}
\label{fig:r-abl}
\end{figure}

\paragraph{Importance.} The LP commitment and flow alone carry 71\% of the split gain, LP features
86\% in total (Figure~\ref{fig:r-gain}). Unit identity (5\%) is how the model learns per-unit
corrections --- e.g.\ that SHOP runs Lio harder than our LP does.

\begin{figure}[H]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=0.62\linewidth]{figures/physics_05_gain_importance.png}
\caption{LP + LightGBM: share of split gain, top 20 features (last walk-forward fold).}
\label{fig:r-gain}
\end{figure}

\paragraph{Contributions.} Split gain counts how much a feature is used in training, not how much it
moves a prediction. TreeSHAP contributions (LightGBM's \texttt{pred\_contrib}) on 20{,}000 validation
rows of the test-like 2021-H2 fold (fold AUC 0.9914) give the per-prediction view
(Figure~\ref{fig:r-contrib}). The LP commitment $u$ moves the log-odds by 2.05 on average, nearly
twice any other feature. Unit identity is second (1.14): it is the channel for per-unit corrections.
Third is the margin, price minus the local water value from the LP duals (0.93), with its 7-hour
rolling mean close behind: the learner reads how far each hour sits from the dispatch threshold,
exactly the graded information a binary schedule discards (Section~\ref{sec:fe-lp}). By group, LP
features carry 70\% of the total absolute contribution, economics 15\%, unit identity and static
attributes 13\%, the observed storage trace 2\% and the constraint series 1\%. Economics weigh more
here than in split gain (15\% against 6\% of the gain in the last fold): many small adjustments
rather than a few decisive splits.

\begin{figure}[H]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=0.95\linewidth]{figures/physics_07_contributions.png}
\caption{LP + LightGBM, 2021-H2 fold: mean absolute TreeSHAP contribution to the log-odds, top 15
features (left) and share by feature group (right).}
\label{fig:r-contrib}
\end{figure}

\paragraph{How the learned layer reads the LP.} The relaxation's $u$ is already roughly a probability
(Figure~\ref{fig:r-lpshop}): SHOP commits in about 1\% of hours where $u=0$ and 94\% where $u=1$, and the
on-rate rises close to the diagonal in between. The departures are unit-specific, which is why unit
identity ranks second. Lio, which SHOP runs to meet the Vest-Vassdraget minimum flow, is committed
in every hour where the LP gives it $u \geq 0.6$ and in three quarters of hours at $0.4$--$0.6$. Hogga,
whose timing is degenerate in our LP when Bandak must fill, is committed in only 45\% of hours at
$u$ between 0.6 and 0.8.

\begin{figure}[H]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=0.68\linewidth]{figures/physics_08_lp_vs_shop.png}
\caption{Share of hours SHOP commits, by the LP relaxation's $u$ in that hour (2021-H2 fold). Dashed:
perfect calibration.}
\label{fig:r-lpshop}
\end{figure}

\paragraph{One week.} Figure~\ref{fig:r-week} shows a test-like case the LP finds harder than three
quarters of its fold. The relaxation spreads Tokke's commitment fractionally over four identical
units and holds Lio at $u \approx 0.45$ until day 3.5. The learned layer concentrates Tokke on G1, the
unit SHOP picks first, and sharpens Lio into the on-block SHOP chose; its within-case AUC is 0.999
against the LP's 0.974. Its remaining error is inherited from the LP: Kjela, on all week in SHOP's
schedule, dips where the relaxation dips (days 4.4--5.6).

\begin{figure}[H]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=0.86\linewidth]{figures/physics_09_example_week.png}
\caption{Case starting 2021-07-02: SHOP's commitment (top), the LP relaxation with no learning
(middle) and the LP + LightGBM probability (bottom), one row per unit, one column per hour.}
\label{fig:r-week}
\end{figure}


\paragraph{The optimiser itself is interpretable.} Its decisions are explained by quantities with
physical meaning: each unit runs when the price exceeds its local water value, which equals its
reservoir's terminal water value unless a constraint binds --- a full reservoir lowers it (water
would otherwise spill), a minimum-flow obligation can force a unit on below it, an empty reservoir
raises it. The three conventions of Section~\ref{sec:fe-lp} are themselves findings about how the
labels were produced.

\subsection{Track C: what the physics features contribute}

The network's own ablation (Section~\ref{sec:fe-phys}) is its interpretation result: removing the 16
physics features costs 0.004 AUC overall and 0.014 on 2021, the year that most resembles the test
period. The features that carry the gain are the ones that encode the same economics as Track B's
LP --- break-even prices from the efficiency curves, the weekly water budget and block profit
against start costs --- computed per plant in closed form instead of jointly by a solver.

\section{Discussion}
\label{sec:r-disc}

\paragraph{Why Track B works.} Track A spent most of its effort recovering, through features, a
decision process that is written down: the spread is the dispatch condition, the count is the
weekly water budget, the block structure comes from start costs, the merit order from penstocks.
Solving the actual problem gets all of these at once, consistently across units and reservoirs,
and extrapolates to unseen price regimes (negative prices, the post-crisis level) from physics
rather than from training data. The learner is left with a smaller, more stationary job: the
residual between our simplified replica and SHOP.

\paragraph{Relation to the task's purpose.} InterOpt wants ML to speed up the optimiser. Our best
model still solves an LP, but one roughly 6--18$\times$ cheaper than SHOP's recorded solve times, and its output is a
calibrated commitment probability that could warm-start SHOP's MIP. Unlike Track A's best
features, it needs no post-decision information.

\paragraph{Limitations and next steps.} The remaining errors are fidelity gaps of the replica: heads
frozen at their initial level, Lio's min-flow behaviour, weeks where SHOP runs units below their
water value (e.g.\ 2019-07-09), and degenerate weeks where a reservoir must fill and the timing of
release is arbitrary. Each fix to the replica feeds the learned layer directly. Three conventions
were read off label statistics that include the validation years; they are structural and stable
across years, but the protocol is not blind to them.

\paragraph{What we would do differently.} Read the topology file on day one. Track A's three
largest late gains were corrections found by reading the documentation; Track B is the same lesson
taken to its conclusion.

\appendix
\section{Reproducibility}
\label{app:repro}

\begin{itemize}
\item \textbf{Configuration.} \texttt{requirements.txt} next to the notebooks pins the package
  versions both notebooks were run with (Short notebook 2 adds PyTorch). The notebooks contain all code, start from the raw
  competition files (\texttt{data/kernel}, \texttt{data/extended}, \texttt{sample\_submission.csv},
  \texttt{prediction\_mapping.csv}), need no network and write only intermediate results (the LP
  cache) and the submission file.
\item \textbf{Short notebook 1} (LP + LightGBM): solves the 3{,}647 LPs in parallel ($\sim$2\,h on 4
  cores, cached after the first run), builds features, trains on all labelled cases and writes the
  submission ($\sim$6\,min, peak $\sim$5\,GB RAM). Executed end to end from the raw data, it
  reproduces the uploaded file to $2\cdot 10^{-13}$, and its LP solutions are byte-identical to the
  stored ones.
\item \textbf{Short notebook 2} (neural network): builds the 99 features from the raw files (about
  1--2 minutes), checks them against values recorded from the original run, and trains three seeds
  on all labelled cases. Its 99 features match the original run's checksums (mean and SD of every
  feature on train and test) to the printed precision. The selected file is the output of the
  executed notebook, run end to end on an Apple M4 GPU (PyTorch 2.15, MPS backend): features in 16\,s,
  the three seeds trained in 32\,min (27--54\,s per epoch). Training is not bit-reproducible, so a
  re-run gives a prediction close to, not identical with, that file. The notebook's last cell shows the
  size of this difference against an earlier upload of the same model: correlation 0.9993, 99.4\% of
  cells on the same side of 0.5, largest single difference 0.33. The total of 84\,min printed in the
  executed notebook includes about 52\,min during which the machine was asleep, visible as three slow epochs of
  seed~1. The notebook uses CUDA,
  then Apple MPS, then the CPU; no GPU is needed: on 4 CPU cores training takes about 2\,h (1.9\,min
  per epoch for 3 seeds $\times$ 20 epochs).
\item \textbf{Track A notebook} (\texttt{notebooks/Track A XGBoost (0.98058).ipynb}, not selected):
  rebuilds our first submission from the raw files (about 40\,min on 4 cores; peak $\sim$24\,GB of
  memory including swap). The uploaded file was produced on an Apple Silicon Mac; on x86 Linux with
  the same package versions the count model selects 143 count features instead of 141, and the
  output correlates 0.995 with the uploaded file.
\item Source modules, every experiment and its result: \texttt{src/}, \texttt{report/leaderboard.md},
  \texttt{report/runs/}.
\end{itemize}
